definitions.definition: When different kinds of evidence from separate fields all point to the same conclusion, making it much more likely to be true.
definitions.example: If a fossil, a DNA test, and a rock layer all show the same age for a dinosaur, that's consilience.

definitions.definition: A perfect one-to-one matching between two things, showing they have the same structure.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system is isomorphic to the actual subway lines if every station and connection matches exactly.

definitions.definition: Standard, accepted, or officially recognized as the correct version.
definitions.example: The 'canonical' way to solve a math problem is the method everyone agrees is correct.

definitions.definition: Conclusions drawn from specific observations to general rules.
definitions.example: Seeing that the sun has risen every day of your life and concluding 'the sun always rises' is an induction.

definitions.definition: The ability of a theory to correctly say what will happen in the future or what new evidence will be found.
definitions.example: Einstein's theory of relativity had predictive power because it predicted that light would bend around the sun, which was later confirmed.

definitions.definition: When separate lines of evidence or arguments come together to point to the same conclusion.
definitions.example: If a detective finds fingerprints, a witness, and a motive all pointing to the same person, that's convergence of evidence.

definitions.definition: Observable events or facts that can be studied.
definitions.example: Rainbows, lightning, and the movement of planets are all natural phenomena.

definitions.definition: A statement or event in the Bible that is believed to be a message from God about the future or about spiritual truth.
definitions.example: Isaiah's prophecy that a virgin would give birth is considered a prophetic witness to Jesus' birth.

definitions.definition: Relating to the origin, structure, and evolution of the entire universe.
definitions.example: The Big Bang theory is a cosmological model of how the universe began.

definitions.definition: A Greek word meaning 'word,' 'reason,' or 'principle.' In the Bible, it refers to Jesus as the divine creative power and order behind the universe.
definitions.example: In the Gospel of John, 'the Word (Logos) was with God, and the Word was God.'

definitions.definition: Something that is unusual, unexpected, or doesn't fit with what is normally observed.
definitions.example: A penguin found in the Sahara desert would be an anomalous sighting.

definitions.definition: Fits together logically or consistently with other facts or ideas.
definitions.example: A good story coheres because all the details make sense together.

definitions.definition: The ability of a belief or theory to reliably lead to true conclusions about reality.
definitions.example: A thermometer that always shows the correct temperature is truth-tracking.

definitions.definition: The art and science of interpreting texts, especially ancient or religious ones.
definitions.example: When reading a 2000-year-old letter, you use hermeneutics to understand what the author meant in their own time.

definitions.definition: Reading your own ideas into a text instead of drawing out what the author actually meant.
definitions.example: Saying a poem about spring is really about aliens is eisegesis — you're forcing your own meaning onto it.

definitions.definition: The study and practice of making dictionaries and defining words.
definitions.example: A lexicographer is someone who decides what words mean and how to list them in a dictionary.

definitions.definition: A study that combines the results of many separate scientific studies to find an overall conclusion.
definitions.example: If ten different studies test a new drug, a meta-analysis looks at all ten together to see if the drug really works.

definitions.definition: Based on observation or experiment, not just theory or logic.
definitions.example: The empirical evidence for gravity is that when you drop a ball, it falls to the ground every time.

definitions.definition: Looking back at past events or data, rather than predicting the future.
definitions.example: A retrospective study might look at old medical records to see if a treatment worked.

definitions.definition: Looking forward to future events or data, often used in predictions or studies that follow people over time.
definitions.example: A prospective study would follow a group of people for ten years to see who gets a disease.

definitions.definition: Describing things as they appear to our senses, not as they actually are in reality.
definitions.example: Saying 'the sun rises' is phenomenological — it describes what we see, even though the sun doesn't actually rise.

definitions.definition: Relating to the nature of being, existence, or reality itself.
definitions.example: An ontological question is 'Does God exist?' — it's about what is real, not just what we see.

definitions.definition: Carefully drawing out the original meaning of a text by studying its language, history, and context.
definitions.example: An exegesis of a Bible verse looks at the original Greek words and the culture of the time to understand what it meant.

definitions.definition: The idea that a scientific theory must be able to be proven wrong by some possible observation or experiment.
definitions.example: The claim 'all swans are white' is falsifiable because finding one black swan would prove it wrong.

definitions.definition: The full set of meanings a word can have in different contexts.
definitions.example: The word 'run' has a wide semantic range: you can run a race, run a business, or run a computer program.

definitions.definition: The region and cultures of the Middle East from around 3000 BC to 300 BC, including Egypt, Mesopotamia, and Israel.
definitions.example: The Ancient Near East is where writing, law codes, and many Bible stories originated.

definitions.definition: A story or theory about how the universe came into existence.
definitions.example: The Big Bang is a scientific cosmogony; the book of Genesis is a religious cosmogony.

definitions.definition: Two words that look or sound similar but have different origins and meanings.
definitions.example: The English word 'embarrassed' and the Spanish word 'embarazada' (pregnant) are false cognates — they look alike but mean different things.

definitions.definition: A way of saying that things are connected by overlapping similarities, not by one single shared feature.
definitions.example: Different games (chess, soccer, solitaire) share a family resemblance — they all involve rules and play, but no one thing is in all of them.

definitions.definition: Taking on a physical body, especially used of God becoming human in Jesus.
definitions.example: In Christianity, Jesus is God incarnate — God in human form.

definitions.definition: A property that does not depend on the specific material or medium it is in.
definitions.example: The information in a book is substrate-independent — it's the same whether printed on paper, displayed on a screen, or spoken aloud.

definitions.definition: The tendency for scientists to publish positive results (that support a hypothesis) more often than negative or null results.
definitions.example: If a drug works, it gets published; if it doesn't, the study might never see the light of day — that's publication bias.

definitions.definition: The study of psychic phenomena like telepathy, clairvoyance, and psychokinesis.
definitions.example: Parapsychology investigates claims like people being able to read minds or move objects with their thoughts.

definitions.definition: The risk of losing respect or credibility in your field by associating with controversial ideas.
definitions.example: A scientist studying UFOs might face reputational costs because other scientists might not take them seriously.

definitions.definition: A comparison between two things that are similar in some way, used to explain or argue.
definitions.example: Saying 'the heart is like a pump' is an analogy that helps explain how blood circulates.

definitions.definition: A basic statement or rule that is accepted as true without proof, used as a starting point for further reasoning.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is an axiom.

definitions.definition: A mathematical model of the universe that describes how it expands uniformly over time, based on Einstein's theory of general relativity.
definitions.example: The FLRW metric is the standard way scientists calculate how the universe has grown since the Big Bang.

definitions.definition: The idea that the act of observing or measuring something can change what is being observed, especially in quantum physics.
definitions.example: In quantum physics, measuring the position of an electron can change its speed — that's the observer effect.

definitions.definition: The branch of physics that deals with the behavior of very tiny particles like atoms and electrons.
definitions.example: Quantum mechanics explains why electrons can be in two places at once, which is impossible in everyday life.

definitions.definition: The idea that something that comes first in time has a special status, like being the original or the cause.
definitions.example: If a student writes a poem and later a famous poet writes something similar, the student has temporal priority.

definitions.definition: A mistake where you treat something as belonging to a type or category it doesn't belong to.
definitions.example: Asking 'What color is the number seven?' is a category error — numbers don't have colors.

definitions.definition: A mistake in reasoning caused by choosing only examples that support your argument and ignoring those that don't.
definitions.example: If you only interview happy customers, you get selection bias — you miss the unhappy ones.

definitions.definition: When a word in one language can be translated into multiple different words in another language, causing confusion.
definitions.example: The Greek word 'logos' can mean 'word,' 'reason,' or 'principle' — that's translation ambiguity.

definitions.definition: A mathematical way to measure how much surprise or uncertainty is in a message, not what the message means.
definitions.example: A coin flip has 1 bit of Shannon information because there are two equally likely outcomes.

definitions.definition: Having the ability to act or make choices, like a person or a conscious being.
definitions.example: A rock is not agentive — it can't decide to roll downhill. A person is agentive because they can choose.

definitions.definition: Disagreed about because of how the study was designed or carried out, not just the results.
definitions.example: A study that doesn't use a control group is methodologically contested because the design is flawed.

definitions.definition: A scientific result that has not been confirmed by other scientists repeating the same experiment.
definitions.example: If only one lab finds a new particle and no one else can, the result is unreplicated and not trusted.

definitions.definition: A measure of how deep a connection is between two ideas — surface level means just words match, deep level means the structure matches.
definitions.example: Saying a car is like a horse because both have 'legs' is surface level; saying both are transportation systems is deeper.

definitions.definition: The ability of a claim to be proven wrong by evidence; a key requirement for a scientific theory.
definitions.example: The claim 'there are invisible unicorns in my garage' is not falsifiable because you can't prove it wrong.

definitions.definition: Groups of related pieces of evidence that together support a claim more strongly than any single piece.
definitions.example: In a trial, a bundle might include a fingerprint, a witness, and a motive — together they are stronger than any one alone.

definitions.definition: When complex patterns or behaviors arise from simple parts interacting, without being planned.
definitions.example: Ant colonies show emergence — no single ant plans the colony, but together they build complex tunnels.

definitions.definition: When something refers to itself, like a sentence that talks about itself.
definitions.example: The sentence 'This sentence is written in English' is self-referential.

definitions.definition: A Hebrew phrase (נוטה שמים) meaning 'stretches out the heavens,' found in the Bible.
definitions.example: In Isaiah, God is described as 'noteh shamayim' — the one who stretches out the sky like a tent.

definitions.definition: A Hebrew verb (נטה) meaning to stretch out, extend, or pitch a tent.
definitions.example: In the Bible, Abraham 'natah' his tent — he pitched it by stretching out the fabric.

definitions.definition: A Hebrew word (רקיע) meaning 'firmament' or 'dome,' referring to the solid sky in ancient cosmology.
definitions.example: In Genesis, God creates a 'raqia' to separate the waters above from the waters below — a solid dome over the earth.
